A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same event-based ADMM research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F report original MNIST, CIFAR-10, regression/LASSO, communication-drop and graph-based learning experiments.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix G report original experimental results, including classifier comparisons, communication counts, regression/LASSO and robustness experiments.

M1.justification: The written Algorithm 1 revises received consensus-value time indices and changes the server proximal residual's +(1-alpha)z_k term to -(1-alpha)z_k. These are limited changes to reported updates; the triggering variants, resets and general Algorithm 2 remain. The PDFs do not establish whether the executed implementation changed.

E1.justification: MNIST, CIFAR-10, synthetic regression/LASSO, graph-based learning and packet-drop scenarios occur in both versions. CIFAR-10's increased client count and revised training budget change settings within retained coverage.

E2.justification: SCAFFOLD is added to the MNIST and regression/LASSO comparisons in v2 Figures 8–9. CIFAR-10 changes from a proposed-method-only curve in v1 Figure 10 to comparisons with FedADMM, FedAvg, FedProx and SCAFFOLD in v2 Figures 3 and 8 and Table 1.

E3.justification: CIFAR-10 changes from 10 to 100 clients, 40 to 150 rounds, eight to three local epochs, and batch size 64 to 20. Its server threshold changes from zero to 0.01 times the client threshold. V2 introduces target-accuracy communication-count comparisons and explicitly labels classifier results as test/validation accuracy; v1 also reported MNIST training loss.

E4.justification: CIFAR-10 gains vanilla-versus-randomized triggering comparisons in v2 Figures 3 and 8, extending the investigation of randomization beyond v1's single CIFAR-10 curve. The reset-period analysis at drop probability 0.3 and the graph communication-strategy comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Table 1 newly states that results average experiments with different random seeds and have standard deviations below 2%, without specifying run counts or individual deviations. V1 has no equivalent seed-reporting statement. Figure 11's minimum–maximum ranges across agents remain in both.

E6.justification: V2 adds target-accuracy communication counts: at 78% CIFAR-10 accuracy, Table 1 reports 18,376 events for randomized triggering, 20,690 for vanilla triggering and 27,000 for FedADMM. It also adds SCAFFOLD results and removes the MNIST training-loss panel. The revised CIFAR-10 results use different settings, so they do not establish a same-setting performance change.

T1.justification: V2 adds Theorem 2.3 and Appendix B, claiming an O(1/K) bound on averaged squared residuals and stationarity terms for potentially nonconvex local objectives with decaying thresholds. Corollary 2.2 also changes its communication-error scaling and restricts the displayed bound to consensus error. The earlier general convex proof is retained in Appendix D.

C1.justification: The abstract expands convergence-analysis claims to nonconvex settings and adds SCAFFOLD to the outperformed baselines. Headline communication savings change from 50% or more to 35% or more, while the conclusion specifies accuracy degradation below 1%. The introduction additionally claims compatibility with compression, quantization and fair aggregation.

C2.justification: V2 adds limitations concerning gradient poisoning, unreliable nodes and the absence of differential-privacy analysis. New discussion addresses bandwidth, latency, asynchronous operation and compression. It also explains SCAFFOLD's communication disadvantage through its additional drift variable and expands discussion of the convexity assumptions.

D1.justification: V2 adds per-target thresholds, triggering probabilities and baseline participation rates in Table 2, plus additional baseline hyperparameters in Tables 3–4. Existing architecture and data-generation descriptions largely carry over. A new inconsistency limits reproducibility: Appendix G specifies CIFAR-10 learning rate 0.001, whereas Table 4 lists 0.01.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands to include SCAFFOLD, FedDC, FedDR, LAG/LENA, adaptive and hierarchical ADMM, and event-triggered model learning and Bayesian optimization. New citations accompany substantive comparisons of participation mechanisms and new positioning relative to compression and quantization.

P1.justification: V2 reorganizes the exposition by moving the Proposition 2.1 and Theorem 4.1 proofs into appendices, integrating CIFAR-10 with the main classifier discussion, and restructuring the experimental appendix. Related-work and experimental passages are extensively revised, and the conclusion gains separate limitations and discussion passages.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one-column to two-column layout. Algorithms and communication diagrams gain coordinated colors, and Figure 2's panels are rearranged. New results/configuration tables and CIFAR-10 trajectories are introduced; classifier trade-off plots are combined, replacing the earlier MNIST loss panel.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens empirical comparisons, reporting and limitations. However, its new nonconvex proof infers global minimization from stationarity before Equation 15 and assumes a saddle point in Equation 19, neither established by Theorem 2.3's assumptions. These concerns affect the newly expanded theoretical claim. Together with conflicting CIFAR-10 learning rates, they prevent a reliable net-quality judgment despite the empirical gains.
